body:
Hi @carlostoledo1891, here's an independent, AI-assisted audit of the λ(4) proof: https://github.com/rainrzk/erdos510-lambda4-audit. As far as I can tell, it doesn't break.

> One small thing on #411: it calls the cubic's root unique, but there are three real roots (≈ −0.1556, 1.0325, 1.5196). λ(4) is the largest.

I redid the computational parts with my own code, using the record only to see what each step claims. The cubic, the 14 generic collisions and all nine families check out, and all 2,231 finite cases re-certify with interval arithmetic. I also swept all 1,473,833 gcd-reduced 4-sets with max ≤ 80 as a sanity check that doesn't use the proof. Nothing beats {1,2,3,4}. The closest is {2,3,4,6}, with min ≈ −1.774.

Caveats: I rebuilt the subfamily parametrizations from the write-up (the finite counts match the record), and I only checked Lemmas A–F by hand.

@rainrzk  Thank you — this is exactly the kind of check the record was published for, and the sweep to max ≤ 80 is a welcome proof-independent control.

Your findings 2 and 3 are correct: the record skips {1,2,3,4} six times (equality cases, once per finite part it lies on — one in d = a+c, three in d = 2b, two in 2d = 2c+b), and §5.8's list omitted cone ii's 89 sets because the listing only picked up single closures. Both are fixed in the write-up, with the skip count now computed from the record so the build refuses if it moves, and the proof page links your audit: https://github.com/carlostoledo1891/cert-machine/commit/1c248ca (paper/lambda4-proof.md, reports/lambda4.html).

Agreed on the roots of the cubic in #411 — λ(4) is the largest of three (≈ −0.1556, 1.0325, 1.5196); the write-up now says so.

On the caveat: Lemmas A–F checked by hand is exactly where a Lean formalization would earn its keep, and I'd be glad to help restructure the record toward one.
